body.text: Southeast Asian leaders yesterday agreed to pursue a policy of “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar’s military-backed government, holding out the possibility of restoring the country’s full membership in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) if it makes progress on the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus framework.

In a joint statement issued after the 49th ASEAN Summit Retreat in Manila, the bloc’s leaders said that they agreed to maintain their policy of excluding Myanmar from participation in ASEAN summits and foreign ministers’ meetings for the time being.

But they said they had agreed to pursue “calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground.” In the event of “sustained and concrete progress” in the implementation of ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC) conflict management plan, leaders said that the bloc “may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation.”

Promulgated in April 2021, two months after a military coup, the 5PC calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to the country’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid. The military junta’s failure to implement the most important points of the Consensus prompted ASEAN to exclude Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings in late 2021.

Ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit and related meetings, which are taking place this week in Manila, ASEAN has come under pressure to loosen the restrictions on Myanmar’s participation in the 11-nation bloc. A growing number of member states have increased their own engagement with Naypyidaw, especially since a new quasi-civilian government took office in April. In that time, five ASEAN member states – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have hosted coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, and pledged their support, explicitly or otherwise, for Myanmar’s reintegration with ASEAN.

While reaffirming the 5PC as the “main reference for addressing the political crisis in Myanmar,” and closing down any prospect of a quick readmission for Min Aung Hlaing’s administration, the region’s leaders yesterday endorsed for the first time bilateral outreach to Myanmar by individual member states. In their statement, the bloc’s leaders said that they tasked foreign ministers “to continue constructive and principled engagement with Myanmar” and “encourage[d] efforts by individual ASEAN Member States through constructive engagement with all relevant stakeholders, in consultation with the ASEAN Chair, to advance substantive progress in the implementation of the 5PC.”

In this respect, yesterday’s statement is an apparent attempt to close the growing gap between ASEAN’s approach to the Myanmar conflict and that of its individual member states. Indeed, the phrase “calibrated engagement” was first coined by Thailand’s government, which has been perhaps the ASEAN member state most active in promoting direct talks with the coup government.

Bangkok has been pursuing this policy since at least 2024, although it has redoubled its efforts since the start of the year, when Myanmar’s military initiated its transition to “civilian” rule. In February, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow declared that Thailand wished to act as “a bridge connecting Myanmar back to ASEAN,” and Thailand helped to organize talks between Myanmar’s foreign minister and his ASEAN colleagues in July – a meeting that Sihasak described as an “icebreaker.” The following month, during Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Thailand, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul affirmed Thailand’s support for the restoration of Myanmar’s membership in ASEAN.
This has created a tension with other member states advocating a more critical position toward Naypyidaw, and even claims that the 5PC had been rendered effectively null.

Yesterday’s statement is an attempt to revive ASEAN’s diplomacy toward Myanmar, and to restore a degree of regional unity via the adoption of a more flexible and pragmatic position. The reference to “developments on the ground” – the phrase appears in two places in the statement – is a seeming admission that events in Myanmar, including momentum in bilateral talks between Naypyidaw and other ASEAN capitals, had begun to outrun the bloc’s own efforts.

This has been something of a leitmotif of the Philippines’ chairmanship this year. During the last ASEAN summit in May, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. admitted that he had not seen “any progress in Myanmar.” In an interview last month, Marcos said that while the 5PC was “absolutely correct,” the bloc needed to try a “new approach” on Myanmar.
On Sunday, in his opening remarks at an ASEAN leaders’ retreat in Manila, Marcos said that “we need to ask ourselves, what more can we do for Myanmar?”

“Myanmar is not merely an issue on ASEAN’s agenda. Myanmar is part of our Asian ASEAN family,” he said. “I hope our session leads to practical and forward-looking discussions on how we can further advance the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, make our efforts more responsive to the realities on the ground, and support a peaceful, inclusive, Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led process,” he said.
After this week’s summit, Philippines is set to hand over the rotating chair of ASEAN to Singapore, which has generally advocated a stricter line on Myanmar.
